fields.expected:
Something my resume doesn't show is how much of my last year has gone into a question that has nothing to do with shipping code. I got interested in why so many capable students around me at Hopkins were moving quickly toward consulting and finance, even when they didn't seem especially interested in the work, and why scientific exploration wasn't competing for those people. So I started reading about how research actually gets funded and selected, from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH and NSF grant model to newer structures like DARPA, ARPA-H, and Focused Research Organizations, and I talked with researchers, research administrators, economists, and science-policy people.

The part I did not expect was how often I was wrong. I went in thinking grant-writing time and compensation were the main constraints. Conversations complicated both. Many researchers consciously trade money for autonomy, and the bigger effect of grant review may be selection: people learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and stop attempting the ones that aren't. I wrote a Substack essay working through that. I like being talked out of a thesis.

fields.expected: I work most with PyTorch and XGBoost for modeling, plus SHAP for interpretation. On the LLM side I've built retrieval-augmented generation pipelines with OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph for memory retrieval, and rubric-driven LLM judging systems where separate judges evaluate dimensions in parallel and then synthesize an evidence-cited assessment. I've also built LLM evaluation frameworks, including comparing model-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. For applied ML systems I've done temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN/Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer, served through a versioned FastAPI microservice. I've also trained a CNN in PyTorch for facial-landmark prediction (~95% PCK), and I use Playwright with OpenAI at narrow, gated call sites for browser automation agents.
